items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the vehicle and traffic law, in relation to compulsory chemical tests
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S3768

TITLE OF BILL:
An act
to amend the vehicle and traffic law, in relation to compulsory
chemical tests

PURPOSE:
The purpose of this bill is to implement a "no refusal" policy in New
York State

SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:
This bill amends the section 1194 of the Vehicle and Traffic Law to
make mandatory the application to a court for an order to compel a
chemical test upon refusal by a motor vehicle operator suspected to
be under the influence to submit to such test.

EXISTING LAW:
Under current law, a police officer or district attorney may apply for
an order to compel upon refusal by an operator to submit to a
chemical test, but are not required to apply.

JUSTIFICATION:
Under current law, upon receipt of his or her driver license a
motorist is deemed to have given consent to submit to a chemical test
when reasonable cause exists to believe he or she is driving under
the influence. Should a motorist choose not to submit, he or she
faces a period license revocation and monetary penalties. Law
enforcement, however, faces the prospect of having to make a case
without what is often times the sole piece of objective evidence in a
DUI case.

Given the choice of a fine and period of revocation as against
providing substantial evidence of one's guilt in what could be a
criminal matter, it is no surprise that many times a motorist refuses
to submit to a chemical test. This legislation seeks to eliminate the
motorist's ability to choose in that instance by requiring that law
enforcement officers seek an order to compel where a motorist has
refused to submit and reasonable cause exists to believe that the
motorist is under the
influence. This bill would add real teeth to the "implied consent"
provision of the Vehicle and Traffic Law.

Under current law, the authority to apply to a court for an order to
compel submission to a chemical test already exists. This bill merely
makes such application mandatory upon a motorist's refusal. All
safeguards remain in place. A law enforcement officer must articulate
to a judge his or her reasonable cause for the belief that the
motorist was driving under the influence, and only when a judge is
satisfied that such cause exists will a court order be issued.

In December, U.S. Transportation Secretary, Ray LaHood highlighted the
need for a national "no refusal" policy, calling on each state to
adopt such a policy. Presently, nine states implement no refusal
strategies at some level. New York's adoption of such a policy would
be a strong tool for law enforcement in the prevention of DUI and DUI
related tragedies.

LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:
New bill.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:
None.

LOCAL FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:
None.

EFFECTIVE DATE:
Immediate.

A.actClause: AN ACT to amend the vehicle and traffic law, in relation to compulsory chemical tests
A.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S3768A

TITLE OF BILL:
An act
to amend the vehicle and traffic law, in relation to compulsory
chemical tests

PURPOSE:
The purpose of this bill is to implement a "no refusal" policy in New
York State

SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:
This bill amends the section 1194 of the Vehicle and Traffic Law to
make mandatory the application to a court for an order to compel a
chemical test upon refusal to submit to a chemical test by a motor
vehicle operator suspected to be under the influence when there has
been a death or serious bodily harm. It also would allow application
to the court in other instances of suspected DUI where the driver
has refused a chemical test.

EXISTING LAW:
Under current law, a police officer or district attorney may apply for
an order to compel upon refusal by an operator to submit to a
chemical test when there is serious bodily harm or death, but are not
required to apply. Law enforcement is not permitted to apply for an
order to compel where there is neither serious bodily harm nor death.

JUSTIFICATION:
Under current law, upon receipt of his or her driver license a
motorist is deemed to have given consent to submit to a chemical test
when reasonable cause exists to believe he or she is driving under
the influence - this is a condition of the privilege to drive. Should
a motorist choose not to submit. he or she faces a period of license
revocation and monetary penalties. Law enforcement, however. faces
the prospect of having to make a case without what is often times the
sole piece of objective evidence in a DUI case.

Given the choice of a fine and period of revocation, as against
providing substantial evidence of one's guilt in what could be a
criminal matter, it is no surprise that many times a motorist refuses
to submit to a chemical test. This legislation seeks to strengthen
law enforcement's hand in these situations. This bill would make
mandatory an application to the court for an order to compel when a
motorist suspected to be under the influence refuses a chemical test
in a situation where there has been death or serious bodily harm.
Additionally, it would allow applications to the court in any
situation in which law enforcement has a reasonable belief that a
motorist is driving under the influence and that motorist has refused
to submit to a chemical test. This bill would add real teeth to the
"implied consent" provision of the Vehicle and Traffic Law.

Presently, the authority to apply to a court for an order to compel
submission to a chemical test exists only in situations of death or
serious injury - and then it is discretionary. This bill makes an
application in such a situations mandatory if a motorist refuses to
submit to a chemical test and there exists a reasonable belief that
the motorist was under the influence. Additionally, present law does
not allow for applications to the court where a motorist refuses to
submit to a chemical test in situations where there is a reasonable
cause exists to believe the motorist is under the influence but in
which there has been no death or serious injury. This bill provides
that authority. In so amending the law, all judicial safeguards have
been preserved. A law enforcement officer must articulate to a judge
his or her reasonable cause for the belief that the motorist was
driving under the influence, and only when a judge is satisfied that
such cause exists will a court order be issued.

In December, U.S. Transportation Secretary, Ray LaHood highlighted the
need for a national "no refusal" policy, calling on each state to
adopt such a policy. Presently, nine states implement no refusal
strategies at some level. New York's adoption of such a policy would
be a strong tool for law enforcement in the prevention of DUI and DUI
related tragedies.

LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:
New bill.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:
None.

LOCAL FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:
None.

EFFECTIVE DATE:
Immediate.
